COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_release_the_republics: In 'Rebuilding Russia' Solzhenitsyn would argue that Russia no longer has the strength to hold the Baltic, the Caucasus and Central Asia against their will. Twenty years earlier, his followers in power reach the same conclusion: better to let these peoples go in peace than to keep spending Russian blood and wealth on an empire that drains its own heartland. Riga, Tbilisi and Tashkent are offered the right to leave.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_the_slavic_question: With the non-Slavic periphery released, a harder question remains: what of Ukraine, Belorussia and the Russian-settled north of Kazakhstan? Solzhenitsyn regards the three East Slavic peoples as branches of a single nation that grew from Kievan Rus. Whether they can be persuaded to stay together with Russia, or whether Russia must learn to stand alone, will define the new state.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_the_slavic_union: Moscow proposes a voluntary union of the Russian, Ukrainian and Belorussian peoples, with Kazakhstan invited to join, bound together by a common faith, history and language rather than by Marxist ideology. Kiev, Minsk and Alma-Ata are free to accept or refuse. If they agree, the old Soviet Union will give way to a smaller and more natural community of kindred nations.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_russia_alone: If the Slavic brothers will not come, Russia will not beg. Solzhenitsyn has always insisted that the Russian people must first heal themselves, and a Russia within her own borders, free of imperial burdens, may yet prove stronger than the sprawling Union ever was. The RSFSR turns inward to rebuild its villages, its churches and its conscience.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_repentance_and_self_limi: In his 1973 essay 'Repentance and Self-Limitation in the Life of Nations', Solzhenitsyn called on Russia to acknowledge the crimes of the Soviet era and to turn away from external expansion toward inner development. The state now adopts this creed as its own: modest ambitions abroad, moral renewal at home and a quiet return to the Orthodox faith and the Russian land.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_directors_take_over: The men who truly run the Soviet economy sit not in the Politburo but in the director's offices of the great combines and ministries. Backed by Interior Minister Nikolai Shchelokov and his MVD, the red directors step out of the shadows and take the reins of government, promising efficiency and prosperity while quietly securing their own share of the people's property.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_shadow_capitalism: Underground workshops, unrecorded production lines and networks of blat have kept Soviet shelves from emptying for decades. Instead of hunting the tsekhoviki and speculators, the new leadership brings them into the light and taxes what was once prosecuted. Critics call it the legalisation of theft; the directors call it realism, and the shadow economy has never been so confident.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_mvd_state: Nikolai Shchelokov has turned the Ministry of Internal Affairs into a power base to rival the KGB, with its own troops, its own informants and its own share of the shadow economy. Under the directors' rule the militsiya becomes the backbone of the state, guarding order on the streets and the interests of its patrons in the ministries.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_model: Two visions of the directors' state compete. The Moscow nomenklatura wants to convert its offices into ownership, turning ministries into holding companies. The republican clans of Tashkent, Baku and Alma-Ata prefer the old ways of patronage, tribute and family loyalty. The directors must decide whose hands will hold the wealth of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_nomenklatura_privatisatio: Ministers become chairmen, departments become concerns, and the officials who once managed state property quietly acquire it. Two decades before it happened historically, the nomenklatura privatises the Soviet economy from within, trading Party cards for share certificates. Productivity may rise, but ordinary citizens begin to ask who now owns the factories they were told belonged to them.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_clan_economy: In the republics, power has long rested on networks of kinship and patronage, from Sharaf Rashidov's Uzbekistan to Dinmukhamed Kunaev's Kazakhstan. Rather than fight these clans, Moscow embraces them: loyal republican bosses receive a free hand and a share of the spoils in exchange for keeping their fiefdoms quiet. Corruption deepens, but the Union holds together.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_cotton_and_caviar: Uzbek cotton and Caspian caviar are worth their weight in hard currency, and both have long been skimmed through padded harvest reports and smuggling rings. The directors stop pretending otherwise and organise these trades for export, channelling the proceeds through friendly hands. The cotton scandal that would historically shake the Party in the 1980s becomes a business model instead.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_directors_banks: Gosbank alone cannot serve the needs of the new economic masters. Enterprise funds and ministry accounts are pooled into commercial banks owned by the directors themselves, lending to friends, financing deals and moving money between the official and the shadow economy. Moscow gains its first modern office blocks, and with them a new class of Soviet bankers.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_western_accounts: The directors know that what the Party gives, the Party can take away. Through Vneshtorgbank, foreign trade missions and front companies in Vienna and Zurich, hard currency flows quietly into private accounts abroad. It is insurance against the next purge, paid for by the Soviet treasury, and it strengthens the shadow economy at the expense of public trust.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_question: The factories have new masters, the banks new owners and the republics new lords. Now the directors must decide what kind of state will protect their gains: an openly governed corporate republic run by managers and bankers, or a populist order that buys social peace with generous handouts. The answer will settle who really owns the Soviet Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_directors_republic: The directors drop the pretence that the Party still governs. Enterprise managers, bankers and ministry chiefs take their seats as the true ruling council of the land, and the state is run like a holding company answerable to its largest shareholders. Profits flow upward, and the language of class struggle gives way to the language of balance sheets.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_buy_the_people: A regime of directors cannot rely on ideology or terror, so it relies on generosity. Higher wages, fuller shops, new flats and better pensions are handed out to keep the workers grateful and quiet while the elite enriches itself. It is an expensive bargain, but the directors calculate that contentment is cheaper than unrest.
COLDWAR_SOV_rd_the_corporate_union: The Soviet Union completes its quiet metamorphosis into a corporate state. The great combines, banks and trading houses now form the skeleton of the country, owned by those who once merely managed them, and the hammer and sickle survives mostly on letterheads. Efficient and profitable, the Corporate Union is also a land where wealth and power belong to very few.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_the_free_enterprise_cabi: A cabinet of young economists around Nikolai Shmelyov, the man who would one day write that the Soviet economy lives on advances and debts, takes office with a radical mandate. Their diagnosis is blunt: the planned economy cannot be repaired, only replaced. Markets, prices and private initiative are to achieve what Gosplan never could, whatever the cost in stability.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_free_the_prices: For decades the state has fixed the price of everything from bread to tractors, and since 1969 a State Committee on Prices has guarded the system, leaving shortages, queues and a thriving black market. The new government abolishes administered prices in one stroke. Shelves will fill again, but for many families the price of a loaf will rise faster than their wages.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_the_rouble_convertible: The Soviet rouble has never been a real currency abroad, its official rate a fiction maintained by Gosbank and the foreign trade monopoly. Making it convertible would tie the Union to world markets, open the door to foreign trade and expose every inefficient enterprise to honest prices. Western bankers are intrigued; the old guard of the Ministry of Foreign Trade is appalled.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_the_speed: The reformers agree on the destination but not on the speed. One camp argues for a single decisive leap, liberalising everything at once before the bureaucracy can regroup. The other warns that a society raised on guaranteed jobs and fixed prices cannot survive such a jolt and urges a gradual transition. The cabinet must choose its pace.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_shock_therapy: Everything at once: prices, trade and enterprises are released in a single blow, as Russia would attempt two decades later in another timeline. The reformers bet that the pain will be sharp but short and that a functioning market will rise from the wreckage of the plan. Factories close, savings evaporate and the streets grow restless, but there is no turning back.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_step_by_step: The cabinet chooses caution over speed. Markets are introduced sector by sector, beginning with services, light industry and agriculture, while heavy industry and basic prices remain under state control for now. Much as Hungary's reformers have done since 1968, the transition is meant to grow out of the plan rather than tear it down, buying time and public patience.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_voucher_privatisation: Two decades before Russia historically tried it, every Soviet citizen receives a voucher, a paper share in the national wealth that can be exchanged for stock in the enterprises being sold off. The idea is to make the people owners and to break the grip of the nomenklatura on state property. Whether workers keep their shares or sell them to the shrewdest bidders remains to be seen.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_open_to_investment: Fiat helped build the great car plant at Togliatti; now the whole Union is open for business. Western firms are invited to set up joint ventures, buy into Soviet enterprises and lend to the state, with legal guarantees that their property will not be nationalised. The capital and technology are badly needed, though the foreign debt that comes with them may one day weigh heavily on Moscow.
COLDWAR_SOV_fel_the_market_union: The planned economy is gone. Prices are set by supply and demand, enterprises answer to owners and customers, and the rouble trades on world markets. The Union that Lenin founded has become something its founders would hardly recognise: a market economy still flying the red flag, prosperous for some, bewildering for many and irreversibly changed.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_the_green_cabinet: Scientists, writers and engineers who have spent years defending Lake Baikal against the planners now find themselves in power. Inspired by the limnologist Grigory Galazy of the Limnological Institute in Irkutsk, the new cabinet declares that the Soviet people must stop conquering nature and start protecting it. Every gigantic project of Gosplan will be judged by a new measure: what it costs the land.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_save_baikal: Since 1966 the Baikalsk Pulp and Paper Mill has poured its waste into the deepest and oldest lake on Earth, home to the nerpa seal and hundreds of species found nowhere else. Scientists and writers across the Union have protested for years. The new government finally orders the mill closed, placing the purity of Baikal above the plan's demand for cellulose.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_stop_the_rivers: Soviet planners dream of reversing the great Siberian rivers, sending the waters of the Ob and Irtysh south through a vast canal to irrigate the cotton fields of Central Asia. Ecologists warn of flooded forests, a changed Arctic climate and drowned villages. The project is cancelled, to the relief of Siberia and the dismay of the Central Asian republics that counted on its water.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_the_path: The Friends of Baikal must decide what kind of movement they are. Some see ecology as the fulfilment of socialism, a planned economy that finally plans for the planet as well as for output. Others simply want to shield nature from industry, whatever the ideology, through strict laws and vast reserves. The choice will shape the green Union to come.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_green_socialism: Planning, the reformers argue, is the perfect tool for ecology if only it aims at the right targets. Gosplan is ordered to account for clean water, forests and air alongside steel and grain, and the Party preaches harmony between man and nature as a socialist virtue. Consumers may wait a little longer for their goods, but their children will inherit a living land.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_conservation_first: The Soviet Union already has its strict nature reserves, some dating back to Lenin's time, but they have long been sacrificed to mines and logging. Now conservation comes first: new reserves are founded, mining is bound by tough environmental rules and no project may proceed without an ecological review. Nature, not output, becomes the first concern of the state.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_save_the_aral: Fed by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, the Aral Sea is already shrinking as Soviet cotton farms drink up its rivers. Hydrologists warn that within a generation it could become a salt desert poisoning Karakalpakstan and Kazakhstan. By curbing irrigation and restoring river flows, Moscow tries to save the sea and wins the gratitude of the peoples who live along its shores.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_close_semipalatinsk: Since 1949 the steppe near Semipalatinsk in Kazakhstan has been the main Soviet nuclear test site, scarred by hundreds of explosions whose fallout has sickened the surrounding villages. Closing the Polygon is a gesture of respect to the Kazakh people and a signal of goodwill to the world, though the generals and the weapons designers protest bitterly at losing their proving ground.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_the_rbmk_question: The RBMK, pride of Soviet nuclear engineering, is cheap to build and can be scaled to enormous size, and the first units are rising at Leningrad. Yet some physicists warn of a dangerous design flaw that could make the reactor run away under the wrong conditions. Heeding them means slower construction and less power, but it may spare a town called Chernobyl a terrible fate.
COLDWAR_SOV_fob_the_green_union: The Soviet Union becomes the first great power to place ecology at the heart of its state ideology. Clean rivers, protected forests and renewable power replace gigantomania as symbols of national pride, and Lake Baikal stands as the emblem of a new relationship between people and land. Abroad, the Green Union offers the world an unexpected vision of what socialism can become.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_the_market_socialists: Alexander Yakovlev, acting head of the Central Committee's propaganda department, has long believed that socialism can be both efficient and humane. With his allies in power, the Soviet Union looks to Budapest and Belgrade rather than to its own dogmas, promising markets within a planned framework, more freedom for enterprises and less fear for citizens: socialism with a human face.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_an_early_glasnost: Fifteen years before Gorbachev made it a watchword, the government embraces glasnost. The censors of Glavlit loosen their grip, newspapers may criticise mismanagement and banned writers return to the pages of Novy Mir. Scientists and engineers welcome the freer exchange of ideas, while the guardians of ideology warn that once people are allowed to speak, they may never stop.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_the_cooperative_law: Instead of prosecuting the shadow economy, the reformers give it a legal form. Citizens may now found cooperatives, small collectively owned businesses running cafes, workshops, repair shops and taxis, as the Law on Cooperation would only allow in 1988 historically. The black market shrinks, services finally appear and a new class of socialist entrepreneurs is born.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_the_model: Two models of reformed socialism lie to the west. Tito's Yugoslavia entrusts its factories to workers' councils that elect managers and share profits. Kádár's Hungary keeps state ownership but frees enterprises to respond to prices and profits under the New Economic Mechanism of 1968. Moscow must decide which experiment to follow on a continental scale.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_self_management: Following the Yugoslav example, Soviet enterprises are handed to the people who work in them. Elected workers' councils appoint directors, set wages and decide how to invest their profits, while the trade unions gain real influence for the first time since the 1920s. Belgrade welcomes Moscow's late conversion to its heresy, and the Soviet worker becomes a co-owner in fact as well as in slogans.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_the_new_mechanism: Hungary's New Economic Mechanism, designed by Rezső Nyers and launched in 1968, keeps the factories in state hands but lets them trade, set many of their own prices and keep their profits. Moscow adopts the model for the whole Union, replacing thousands of plan targets with a few broad guidelines. Kádár's quiet goulash communism becomes the blueprint for a superpower.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_open_to_the_world: A socialism that can compete need not hide behind walls. Trade barriers come down, joint ventures with Western firms are encouraged and Soviet scientists, artists and tourists travel abroad more freely. Detente gains a new depth as the West discovers a Soviet Union more interested in exchange than in confrontation, and tensions between the blocs begin to ease.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_federal_reform: The Union has always been federal on paper and centralist in practice. The reformers take the constitution at its word, transferring real powers over budgets, culture and local industry from the Moscow ministries to the fifteen union republics. National elites gain a stake in the reformed Union, and the old charge of Russian domination loses some of its sting.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_the_question: Market socialism has transformed the Soviet economy, but its architects disagree on where to stop. One faction wants to keep the commanding heights in public hands, with markets serving a socialist plan. The other argues that half-measures breed stagnation and that private property must be allowed to grow alongside the state. The reformers must decide how far the market may go.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_socialist_market: The reform stops at the gates of private ownership. Enterprises compete, prices move and managers answer for profits, but the land, the banks and the great industries remain the property of society. It is a balance that Lenin's New Economic Policy once struck and Stalin abolished, now restored as the permanent foundation of Soviet socialism.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_the_mixed_economy: The reformers go further than any socialist state before them. Private businesses may grow beyond family workshops, foreign capital may own shares and the state keeps only the strategic industries in its hands. Purists in the Party denounce a betrayal of October, but the result resembles the mixed economies of Western Europe more than anything Marx described.
COLDWAR_SOV_smc_the_commonwealth: The Socialist Market Commonwealth is complete: a voluntary association of reformed republics bound by a common market, shared institutions and a socialism that has learned to trust its citizens. The Soviet Union has become what the Prague reformers dreamed of in 1968, a state where economic freedom and social justice coexist. Whether the world believes it is another matter.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_a_union_of_sovereign_rep: Pyotr Shelest, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, has long defended the language, culture and economic interests of his republic against Moscow's centralism. With his allies now leading the Union, a new idea takes hold: national communism, in which each republic builds socialism in its own way within a loose union of sovereign Soviet states.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_the_new_union_treaty: The Treaty of 1922 that created the Soviet Union is to be replaced by a new compact among equals. Each union republic is invited to sign, gaining wider powers over its economy, language and internal affairs while remaining within a common state. It is the bargain Gorbachev would offer too late in 1991, proposed while the Union is still strong enough to make it work.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_our_soviet_ukraine: Named after Shelest's 1970 book 'O Ukraine, Our Soviet Land', this programme celebrates Ukraine as a full partner in the Union rather than a province of Moscow. The Ukrainian language returns to schools, universities and publishing houses, Cossack history is honoured and Kiev gains a greater say over the republic's coal, steel and grain. Ukrainians answer with growing loyalty to the reformed Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_the_model: The national communists disagree on the shape of the new Union. Some want every republic, from Estonia to Tajikistan, to follow its own road to socialism as an equal partner. Others believe the Union needs a new core and look to an axis between Moscow and Kiev, with Ukraine as the second pillar of the federation. Shelest's followers must choose.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_many_paths: Lenin's policy of korenizatsiya, the rooting of Soviet power in each nation's own language and cadres, is revived after decades of Russification. Every republic is free to adapt socialism to its own traditions, from the collective farms of the Baltic to the cotton fields of Uzbekistan. The Union becomes a family of distinct nations rather than a single Soviet people.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_the_kiev_axis: Russia and Ukraine together form the heart of the Union, and the national communists propose to make this partnership explicit. Kiev becomes a second capital, Ukrainian cadres take a larger share of leading posts in Moscow and the two largest republics jointly steer the federation. The smaller republics grumble at a new dual hegemony, but the Union gains a firmer core.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_economic_sovereignty: Republican governments take control of the enterprises on their territory, much as Khrushchev's regional economic councils, the sovnarkhozy, attempted in 1957. The ministries in Moscow lose their grip, and local planners who know their own resources can finally act without waiting for permission. Productivity rises as each republic competes to show what it can achieve on its own.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_republic_formations: During the Great Patriotic War the Red Army fielded national divisions raised in the republics, until they were quietly disbanded after the victory. The national communists revive the idea: each republic raises formations of its own citizens, commanded in their own languages but sworn to the common defence. The army grows, and so does the republics' sense of ownership in it.
COLDWAR_SOV_usr_the_commonwealth_of_sovi: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics gives way to a Commonwealth of Soviet States, a voluntary association of sovereign socialist nations sharing a common defence, currency and market. Unlike the hasty Commonwealth of Independent States of 1991, it is built while trust between the republics still exists. Nationalist passions cool, for every nation now has its own state within the family.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_russian_party: Within the Party apparatus an informal current has grown that values Russian tradition above Marxist internationalism. Its patron is Politburo member Dmitry Polyansky, its voice the journal Molodaya Gvardiya, and its supporters reach from the Komsomol to the Writers' Union. Now the 'Russian Party' steps into the open, determined to put the Russian people first in the state they built.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_molodaya_gvardiya_lin: Under its editor Anatoly Nikonov, Molodaya Gvardiya has printed essays praising the Russian village, the Orthodox heritage and the national spirit, drawing fierce condemnation from Party liberals. Its line now becomes official policy: the press, the publishing houses and the Komsomol are encouraged to promote Russian patriotism, and the guardians of ideology learn to speak of the nation as readily as of class.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_russian_village_first: The village prose of Vasily Belov and Valentin Rasputin mourns the dying Russian countryside, its churches in ruins and its young people fleeing to the cities. The Russian Party makes the revival of the Non-Black Earth Zone a national priority, pouring money into roads, housing and machinery for the old Russian heartland that collectivisation left behind.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_model: The Russian Party is united in its love of Russia but divided over her past. The red wing honours the Soviet state as the latest form of Russian greatness and seeks to fuse Bolshevism with national pride. The white wing looks further back, to Orthodoxy, old Russia and the faith that sustained the people before 1917. One vision must prevail.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_national_bolshevism: The ideas of Nikolai Ustryalov, who saw in Bolshevism a new incarnation of the Russian state, find fresh followers. The Soviet Union is presented as the heir to a thousand years of Russian history and the Party as its rightful guardian. Communist symbols and Russian patriotism merge into a single creed of red greatness that appeals to soldiers and workers alike.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_orthodox_nationalism: The white wing of the Russian Party wins out. The persecution of the Church ends, the Moscow Patriarchate gains a voice in public life and restored churches ring their bells again across Russia. Faith is recast as the soul of the nation and the Church becomes a pillar of the state, an arrangement unthinkable to the militantly atheist Party of only a few years before.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_a_communist_party_for_the: Every union republic has its own Communist Party except the largest, Russia, whose affairs are run directly by the all-Union apparatus. The Russian Party demands an end to this anomaly and founds a Communist Party of the RSFSR with its own Central Committee. Russians gain an institution of their own, while the other republics fear it as a rival centre of power.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_slavic_core: Russia, Ukraine and Belorussia share a common origin in Kievan Rus, and the Russian Party wants their bond to be closer than that with any other republic. Kiev and Minsk are offered a privileged partnership: deeper integration with Russia in exchange for continued autonomy and respect for their own languages. The Slavic core is meant to become the unbreakable heart of the state.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_great_power_army: The Soviet Army is honoured as the heir of Suvorov and Kutuzov, of Borodino and Stalingrad, and its traditions are tied ever more openly to Russian history. Officers are told they defend Russia first and ideology second, and the General Staff welcomes the new prestige and budget. A proud army, the Russian Party believes, is the backbone of a great power.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_question: The Russian Party faces its oldest dilemma. Should Russia hold the Union together as an empire, carrying the burden of the borderlands for the sake of greatness? Or should she shed the periphery and become a compact nation-state, spending her strength on her own people? Imperial patriots and the followers of Solzhenitsyn give opposite answers, and the Party must choose.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_empire: Russia chooses greatness. The Union is to be held together at any price, its borderlands bound to Moscow by Russian settlers, the Russian language and Russian bayonets. The patriotic press speaks of a historic mission, and the militsiya grows to keep the realm secure. The empire endures, but its peoples are reminded daily who is the elder brother.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_the_nation: Russia chooses herself. The costly subsidies to the borderlands are cut, the republics are allowed to drift toward independence and the state concentrates on the Russian lands, from Smolensk to Vladivostok. Many imperial patriots call it a betrayal, but ordinary Russians welcome a government that finally spends the nation's wealth at home.
COLDWAR_SOV_rp_great_russia: The Russian Party completes its programme. Soviet achievement and Russian tradition, the space rockets and the onion domes, the victory of 1945 and the memory of Kutuzov stand side by side in a new national synthesis. Great Russia is confident, patriotic and proud of her thousand-year history, and her people believe once more that they are destined to shape the world.
COLDWAR_SOV_cnr_the_national_rebirth: From the shadows of the Union, a clandestine committee of embittered officers, writers and officials has prepared for this hour. Rejecting both communism and the West, they promise the national rebirth of a Russian people they believe has been betrayed by internationalists and bureaucrats. Their rule begins with emergency decrees, closed borders and a hunt for enemies within.
COLDWAR_SOV_cnr_the_emergency_committee: Power is placed in the hands of a State Committee for the National Emergency, a collective body that answers to no Congress and no Politburo. Ministers are dismissed, Party officials arrested and the old nomenklatura stripped of its privileges overnight. The committee rules by decree, and the fear it inspires in the elite is matched by the hope it awakens among the angry and the dispossessed.
COLDWAR_SOV_cnr_militarise_the_nation: The Committee declares that a reborn nation must be an armed nation. Military spending climbs, reserve call-ups are extended, and schools, factories and youth organisations are reorganised along military lines. Every citizen is told that the motherland faces enemies on every side, and the whole country begins to take on the look of a vast barracks.
COLDWAR_SOV_cnr_the_path: The leaders of the Committee agree that Russia has been humiliated, but not on how to restore her pride. One faction wants to seal the borders and build an autarkic fortress, immune to Western influence and self-sufficient in everything. The other dreams of revenge and of reclaiming lost influence by force. The direction of the rebirth must now be decided.
COLDWAR_SOV_cnr_fortress_russia: The borders close. Foreign trade is reduced to what is strictly necessary, Western radio is jammed more heavily than ever and unauthorised contact with foreigners becomes a crime. Behind its walls the nation is to produce everything it needs and defend every inch of its soil. Fortress Russia trades prosperity for a security its rulers consider absolute.
COLDWAR_SOV_cnr_the_revanche: The Committee speaks openly of revenge for every retreat and every humiliation the Russian nation has suffered. Troops move toward the frontiers, military doctrine turns to the offensive and the propaganda machine prepares the population for war. The world watches with alarm as Moscow rattles its sabre louder than at any time since the Cuban crisis.
COLDWAR_SOV_cnr_the_rebirth_state: The national rebirth is enshrined as the permanent order of the state. A collective dictatorship of the Committee rules over a disciplined, militarised and inward-looking society in which loyalty to the nation outweighs every other value. Scientists and artists chafe under the new orthodoxy, but the regime has achieved what it set out to do: a Russia remade in its own image.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_marshals_govern: Defence Minister Marshal Andrei Grechko and the senior commanders of the Soviet Armed Forces have lost patience with the quarrelling civilians of the Politburo. Backed by the military districts and the General Staff, they assume direct control of the state through a Council of Marshals. The Party is not abolished, but for the first time since the Revolution it takes its orders from the army.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_general_staff_govern: The General Staff, long called the brain of the army, becomes the brain of the state. Its officers take over ministries and planning bodies, applying the methods of military staff work to the economy and the administration. Decisions are made faster and orders followed more strictly, but civilian expertise is pushed aside in favour of the soldier's way of thinking.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_order_and_discipline: The marshals bring the values of the barracks to civilian life. Absenteeism, drunkenness at work and petty theft are punished severely, corrupt officials face military tribunals and the black marketeers find their protectors gone. Ordinary citizens grumble at the harsh new rules, yet many admit that the trains run on time and the shops are less empty than before.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_model: The officer corps is split between generations. The old marshals who fought from Moscow to Berlin trust in mass armies, vast reserves and the lessons of 1945. Younger reformers around Nikolai Ogarkov, first deputy chief of the General Staff, foresee a revolution in warfare driven by computers, precision weapons and automated command. The Council must decide whose vision will guide the army.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_modernisers: Ogarkov's vision prevails. Military research institutes receive priority funding for electronics, computers and automated command and control, and the army begins to plan for a war fought with reconnaissance-strike complexes rather than endless waves of tanks. The West will one day call it the revolution in military affairs; the Soviet Union now intends to lead it.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_old_marshals: The veterans of the Great Patriotic War keep their grip on the army. Their faith lies in mass, in the deep reserves of the Soviet people and in the armoured fists that once broke the Wehrmacht. Conscription is widened, reserve divisions are filled and the army prepares to fight the next war as it won the last, with numbers, steel and endurance.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_military_economy: The Soviet economy has always served the army first, but under the marshals the defence industry takes direct control of the plan. The Military-Industrial Commission sets priorities for the ministries, new arms plants rise in the Urals and Siberia, and civilian production is subordinated to the needs of defence. Tanks roll off the lines while the shops wait their turn.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_defence_council: The Defence Council of the USSR, once a secretive body chaired by the General Secretary, becomes the supreme organ of state power. Military planning, foreign policy and the economy are now coordinated in a single room by the marshals and their chosen civilians. Decisions that once took months of Politburo bargaining are taken in a single sitting.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_strategic_deterrence: The Strategic Rocket Forces, the youngest and most prestigious branch of the Soviet military, receive the full backing of the marshals. New generations of heavy intercontinental missiles are ordered from the design bureaus of Mikhail Yangel and Vladimir Chelomei, and silos multiply across the steppe. The Council intends to negotiate with Washington from a position of overwhelming strength, whatever the cost to detente.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_question: Military rule was meant to be temporary, a remedy for a crisis the civilians could not handle. Now the marshals face the question every junta eventually confronts. Some argue that order has been restored and the army should return power to the Party before politics corrupts it. Others believe the country needs the soldiers' firm hand indefinitely.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_return_to_the_barracks: Their task complete, the marshals hand power back to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and return to their headquarters. The army keeps its prestige and a powerful voice in matters of defence, but the principle of Party control over the military is restored. The soldiers have shown that they can rule, and the Party will not forget it.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_permanent_stavka: During the Great Patriotic War the Stavka of the Supreme High Command directed the entire Soviet war effort. The marshals now make it a permanent institution of peacetime government, a supreme headquarters that commands not only armies but ministries and republics. The Soviet Union becomes a state permanently organised for war, whether war comes or not.
COLDWAR_SOV_com_the_garrison_state: The rule of the marshals hardens into a lasting order. Every region is a military district, every factory a potential arsenal and every citizen a soldier in reserve. Shielded by its nuclear arsenal and its vast armies, the Garrison State offers its people security and discipline in place of freedom, and the world must reckon with a superpower ruled by its generals.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_return_of_the_tsar: Few would have believed it possible: in a Soviet Union shaken by crisis, the head of the House of Romanov, Grand Duke Vladimir Kirillovich, is invited back from exile in Madrid. Born in Finland in 1917 and raised in emigration, he has never seen the Russia he claims. Monarchists, nationalists and many weary citizens now look to him as the symbol of a lost continuity.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_coronation: For the first time since 1896, a Russian emperor is crowned in the Dormition Cathedral of the Moscow Kremlin. The ancient regalia are brought out of the Armoury, the bells of Ivan the Great ring out and crowds fill Red Square, some in joy, some in disbelief. Whatever the future holds, the coronation of Vladimir Kirillovich marks a break with more than half a century of Soviet history.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_church_and_the_crown: Tsar and Patriarch were once the twin pillars of Holy Russia, and the restored monarchy seeks to rebuild that alliance. The Moscow Patriarchate is freed from Soviet supervision, its seminaries and monasteries reopen and plans are drawn up to rebuild the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. The Church in turn blesses the crown and calls on the faithful to support it.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_form: What kind of monarchy will Russia have? Liberal monarchists point to the State Duma of 1906 and to the constitutional crowns of Britain and Scandinavia. Traditionalists insist that only an autocrat, ruling by the grace of God as the tsars once did, can hold the vast country together after decades of upheaval. The Grand Duke and his advisers must settle the question.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_constitutional_monarchy: The emperor reigns but does not rule. A new State Duma is elected by the people, a constitution guarantees civil rights and the government answers to parliament. Russia picks up the thread of the reforms of 1905 that war and revolution cut short, and Western capitals watch with fascination as the largest country on Earth becomes a parliamentary monarchy.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_autocrat: The old formula of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality is revived. The emperor rules with full authority, assisted by ministers he alone appoints, and the Soviet instruments of control are turned to the service of the throne. Supporters see a return to the natural order of Russian life; opponents note that the new autocracy relies on the same secret police as the old dictatorship.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_emigres_return: In Paris, Berlin, Belgrade, New York and Buenos Aires, the descendants of the White emigration have kept Russian culture alive in exile for half a century. Now they are invited home. Engineers, scholars, priests and businessmen return with knowledge, capital and connections abroad, and Russia rediscovers a part of herself that the Revolution scattered across the world.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_crown_and_the_republ: The restored monarchy inherits fifteen union republics that owe no loyalty to a Russian tsar. Georgians, Balts and Central Asians watch the coronation with suspicion, and many remember the old empire as a prison of nations. The crown offers the republics broad self-government under the dynasty, but some prefer to drift away rather than kneel before a Romanov.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_royal_houses: The Romanovs are bound by blood to nearly every royal house in Europe, and the Grand Duke has lived for years in Madrid. His envoys now call on Buckingham Palace and on Prince Juan Carlos, seeking recognition of the restored crown. For London and Madrid, embracing a Russian emperor would be a remarkable gesture, and a useful wedge between Moscow and its communist past.
COLDWAR_SOV_rom_the_restored_empire: The double-headed eagle flies once again over the Kremlin. The Russian Empire, abolished in 1917, has risen from the ruins of the Soviet experiment, with a Romanov on the throne and the Church at his side. It is a different empire from the one Nicholas II lost, shaped by decades of Soviet industry and education, but it claims the same thousand-year inheritance.
